planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun against a warm wall or border for best flowering.

directions: Set bulbs shallowly, with the tip barely covered, in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally at the base of a warm south-facing wall that mimics its native rocky Drakensberg slopes. Mark Fenwick is a long-cultivated, deep rose-pink selection of the hardiest nerine species, prized for producing unusually large flower heads with more blooms per umbel than the wild form, borne on sturdy bare stalks in early to mid autumn before the strappy leaves emerge. Leave clumps undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as bulbs become congested, and withhold summer water once the foliage dies back to respect its dry dormancy. Where winters are wetter or colder than zone 7 allows, mulch heavily in fall or grow in pots that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck just above soil level in spring in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; give a sheltered site in the coldest end of its range.

directions: Plant with the bulb neck exposed at the soil surface in sharply drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, and avoid summer irrigation once foliage dies back. This white-flowered selection of the hardiest Cape nerine carries the same reflexed, crinkle-edged, spidery blooms as the species but in clean white rather than pink, opening on bare stems in early to mid autumn ahead of the strap-shaped leaves. Because it flowers well only once clumps are established and slightly pot-bound, resist dividing for several years and top-dress lightly with a low-nitrogen bulb fertilizer each spring. In borderline zone-7 gardens a dry winter mulch of grit or bracken protects the crowns from prolonged wet cold.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest burgundy leaf color.

directions: Plant bulbs about four to five inches deep after danger of frost has passed, in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil; strong sun brings out the darkest foliage color, while too much shade fades the purple to green. This RHS Award of Garden Merit cultivar forms a rosette of glossy, wine-purple strap leaves from which a thick, similarly dark-flushed spike rises in mid to late summer, packed with small starry flowers in dusky maroon-pink and topped with the pineapple-like tuft of bracts. It combines striking foliage color with the long bloom season typical of the species and pairs well with silver or chartreuse companions in a border or large container. Keep soil consistently moist through active growth, taper off as leaves yellow in fall, and mulch heavily over winter in zone 7-8 gardens or lift and store where winters are more severe.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; a compact, deep-burgundy-leaved selection well suited to containers.

directions: Plant bulbs roughly four inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, siting in full sun to develop the richest maroon-purple leaf color. A Plant Delights Nursery introduction and sport-selection related to 'Sparkling Burgundy', Oakhurst is more compact and heavily substanced in the leaf, holding its dark color from spring emergence through the summer bloom spike of small maroon-pink, star-shaped flowers crowned by the characteristic leafy top-knot. Its shorter stature makes it a good candidate for the front of a border or a large patio pot where its foliage color can be appreciated up close. Water regularly through summer, reduce as foliage declines in fall, and protect the dormant bulb from hard freezes with a thick mulch or by lifting in colder zones.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this species produces small bulbils along the flower stem in addition to underground corms and can naturalize readily in mild climates.

directions: Plant corms three to four inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to light shade; the corms establish roots over the cool season and send up sword-shaped, iris-like fans of foliage ahead of spring bloom. Watsonia meriana produces branched spikes of funnel-shaped flowers, usually in shades of salmon-pink to orange-red, opening progressively up the stem over several weeks, and is notable among watsonias for forming small aerial bulbils along the upper stem in addition to its underground corms, a trait that lets it spread and colonize readily in favorable climates. After flowering the foliage dies back for a dry summer dormancy; withhold irrigation during this period to prevent corm rot. Because it can naturalize aggressively in mild, moist coastal climates, site it where spread is welcome or remove spent bulbil-bearing stems before they root.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free areas (zones 9-10) or start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost in cold climates; a classic violet-blue fragrant freesia cultivar.

directions: Plant corms about two inches deep and two to three inches apart in gritty, well-drained soil, since freesias are prone to rot in wet conditions, especially once they finish flowering. Royal Blue is a long-grown, richly scented cultivar bearing funnel-shaped flowers in deep violet-blue with a contrasting pale throat, carried on the same slender, arching stems and narrow sword-like foliage typical of florists' freesias. The wiry stems tend to flop under the weight of the flower spikes and benefit from twiggy brush support or a grow-through grid. In frost-free gardens the corms persist and can be left in the ground to naturalize; elsewhere lift after the foliage yellows, cure thoroughly, and store dry and cool until fall replanting.
